units.title: Live: the storm, day two
units.author: soundfm
units.text: 06:15. Good morning. The worst of the night is behind us, though the amber warning stays in force until midday and the wind is still gusting near 50 knots on the coast. Carrow Point reports a peak gust overnight of more than 60 knots just before midnight. We'll be bringing you roads, power, schools and ferries through the morning.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 06:50. Schools: Tollinby Primary, Brackwater Primary and the Lisle school are closed again today. All three expect to open tomorrow. The Port Ammet secondary is open for pupils who can get there safely; the bus from Gilliver is running about forty minutes late because of debris on the harbour road.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 07:45. Power: Sound Power Co-op says about 700 properties are still off, mainly on the Brackwater ridge and east of Tollinby. Crews worked through the night where gusts allowed and restored supply to the care home on Station Road just after 01:00. Gilliver and Port Ammet supplies held throughout the storm.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 08:40. Roads: the Tollinby road has reopened at the garden centre dip, where a car was stranded yesterday. The lower Tollinby road is now closed at Mill Bridge after part of the verge slipped into the beck overnight. The Brackwater ridge road remains closed near Holly Lane, and the Carrow Point road is still shut.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 09:35. Ferries: Sound Lines will try a single sailing from Port Ammet to Lisle and Gilliver at midday if an inspection of the Lisle slip this morning is satisfactory. There will be no morning sailings. The company says it will publish the rest of today's timetable by 10:00.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 10:50. In Gilliver, harbour users are sweeping weed and stones off the harbour road after waves overtopped the sea wall on two high tides. Three coping stones have come off the wall by the lifeboat house. The harbour has reopened to essential movements, but the slipway stays closed until it has been inspected.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 12:20. The midday ferry has sailed from Port Ammet, about forty minutes late. Passengers at the terminal applauded when it pulled away. The skipper reported a heavy swell at the Lisle approach. Sound Lines says afternoon sailings will run subject to conditions, but tonight's late crossings are under review.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 13:40. The Met Office has replaced the amber warning with a yellow warning, valid until midday tomorrow. Forecasters expect a quieter spell this evening, followed by a further band of strong westerly winds and showers from the early hours. They're asking people not to take the lull as the end of it.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 15:00. Listeners' pictures from the clean-up: a shed that has travelled to the end of its garden and is now leaning on the fence like it's chatting to the neighbours; a pallet of white and blue fenders spread along the beach below Gilliver; and a florist in Port Ammet sweeping petals off Tanner Street.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 16:45. Power update: around 450 properties remain without supply. The co-op says the last of the Tollinby faults should be cleared tonight, but some homes on the Brackwater ridge, where two poles are down across the lane, may not be reconnected until tomorrow. Brackwater village hall stays open as a warm space until 22:00.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 18:30. Port Ammet General says it has treated more than thirty people for storm-related injuries since yesterday morning, almost all minor: cuts, sprains and one broken wrist from a man who tried to hold on to a trampoline. Staff thanked the public for staying away from A&E with anything that could wait.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: 20:15. We're closing the live page for tonight. The wind has dropped to almost nothing in places, but forecasters expect it back after 03:00. Tomorrow: schools expected open; ferry decisions at 06:00; council crews will start on the Mill Bridge slip at first light. Thank you for everything you've sent us. Goodnight.

units.title: Storm: the clear-up begins across the Sound
units.author: courier
units.text: Council crews, linesmen and volunteers began clearing up across the Marrow Sound today after the strongest gale in years brought down trees, cut power to more than a thousand homes and left the Gilliver harbour road strewn with stones. The storm is not over: forecasters expect a further spell of strong winds tomorrow before it clears.

units.author: courier
units.text: At its height, just before midnight, a gust of more than 60 knots was recorded at Carrow Point. In Brackwater, where the overflow channel at the reservoir began running, the estate ranger closed the woods to the public, saying fallen trees and loose limbs made them dangerous even in daylight.

units.author: courier
units.text: Sound Power Co-op said around 1,300 properties lost supply at some point, most of them in Brackwater and Tollinby. Gilliver and Port Ammet were barely affected. 'The Gilliver line just sat there and took it,' one lineman said. 'It's an awkward old line most of the year. This time it behaved.'

units.author: courier
units.text: In Weyhaven, Port Ammet and Tollinby, residents described neighbours carrying water up tower blocks, a stranded driver who waited on the roof of his car with a packet of crisps, and a mystery helper who waved drivers round the flooded dip in the Tollinby road on the worst night. The Courier would like to hear from them.

units.author: courier
units.text: The council asks residents to report fallen trees on public land through its website rather than by phone, and reminds householders that trees on private land are their own responsibility. Storm-damaged trees can be dangerous to cut; the council recommends using an insured contractor.

units.title: Holm crew sat out storm, contractor says
units.author: courier
units.text: The crew clearing Kittering Holm sat out the storm in their site camp, according to Grieve Land Services, which holds the contract. A spokesperson said work had been 'paused for safety, as it would be on any site', and that the company was in contact with its site lead throughout.

units.author: courier
units.text: No boats crossed to the Holm on either day of the storm. Gilliver fishermen said the island was hidden by spray for most of yesterday afternoon. One said that when it reappeared this morning it 'looked just the same from here, which it would'.

units.author: courier
units.text: Grieve declined to say whether the storm would affect the thirty-day completion date, repeating that the job was 'proceeding to schedule'. Ardent Vale Holdings, the island's owner, did not respond to the Courier's questions. It has not answered any of the questions put to it since this newspaper first reported on the clearance.

units.title: Quayside streets flood as surge meets high tide
units.author: weypost
units.text: Seawater flooded several streets around Weyhaven's old quayside on this morning's high tide as a storm surge combined with spring tides. Water reached ankle depth on Ropemakers Row and the bottom of Quay Road, and several ground-floor businesses were flooded.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The owner of a noodle bar on Ropemakers Row said she had moved her stock upstairs the night before after reading the forecast. 'We lost the doormat and a lot of patience,' she said. 'The kitchen's dry. We'll be open tomorrow if the electrician says yes.'

units.author: weypost
units.text: The city council said the quayside flood gates had been closed but that water came through drains that back up at high tide, a known problem it has asked for funding to fix. Sandbags have been delivered to affected businesses and the council's drainage team is pumping out the worst-hit cellars.

units.author: weypost
units.text: The container port reopened at 11:00 after gusts dropped below the cranes' limit. Lorries queued back along the port road for most of the afternoon as hauliers tried to clear two days of backlog.

units.title: Lifts return block by block as residents count the cost
units.author: weypost
units.text: Lifts in most of Weyhaven's tower blocks were back in service by lunchtime today after a day and a half out of action. Several blocks reported broken landing windows, and one managing agent said contractors would board them 'when conditions permit'.

units.author: weypost
units.text: Residents' associations praised neighbours who carried water and shopping to upper floors and checked on older tenants. One association secretary said: 'The lifts are back and the windows will be fixed eventually. What I'll remember is who knocked on whose door.'

units.author: weypost
units.text: The city council said it would review how landlords contact residents with mobility needs during lift shutdowns, after several complaints that vulnerable tenants were not told in advance. Its emergency line handled more than six hundred calls over the two days.

units.title: Storm windthrow set to flood timber market
units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Early reports from forest managers across the north of the region suggest the storm has caused significant windthrow in exposed plantations, particularly on shallow soils near the coast. One manager estimated that a single compartment of mature spruce had lost a third of its stems overnight.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: Merchants expect a rise in the supply of storm-felled softwood over the winter, which could push down prices for sawlogs and pulp. Firms with cut timber already stacked, including contractors on coastal clearance jobs, may find buyers harder to come by and slower to pay.

units.author: tradejournal
units.text: The safety council has reminded contractors that windthrow clearance is specialist work. Root plates under tension, hung-up stems and broken tops cause a disproportionate share of serious accidents every winter. 'The trees that are already down are the dangerous ones,' its chair said. 'Take them slowly.'

units.title: Overnight show: two nights of storm calls
units.author: soundfm
units.text: Sound FM's overnight show stayed on air throughout the storm on generator power, taking calls from listeners without electricity across the Sound. The producer said the most common call was not about damage at all but from people who simply wanted to hear another voice while the wind was at its worst.

units.author: soundfm
units.text: Callers included a woman in Lisle who found her tomato plants, still in their pots, two gardens away, and a caller from abroad trying to find out whether her father's power was back on in Brackwater. It was, at ten past ten. The show resumes its normal running order tonight.

units.title: Pay period 3 opened
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Pay period 3 has opened for contract Kittering Holm (contract days 15 to 21). Day-rate liabilities are raised at nightly settlement as normal. Storm days are recorded as days on site. Your statement for period 3 will be issued at the end of contract day 21. This is an automated message. Please do not reply to this address; it is not monitored.

units.title: Reminder: balance carried forward (ref GLS-KH-1501)
units.author: grieve_payroll
units.text: Reminder. Reference: GLS-KH-1501. An outstanding crew wage balance has been carried forward from pay period 2 into period 3. Operations has been notified. Settle at the site terminal at the earliest opportunity; payments clear the oldest liabilities first. This is an automated message. Replies to this address are not read.

units.title: Storm, day two
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text:
Hi,
- The Met Office has the warning on until midday, then a yellow one; there's a lull forecast tonight and more wind from the early hours.
- The supply skipper won't cross today. He hopes for tomorrow afternoon, weather permitting; orders still roll to his next crossing.
- No felling while the wind is up. If the lull comes, use it to check the camp, not the count.
- Just checking where we are on numbers, when you have a moment.
Thanks, Ruth

units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, end-of-day note. I've spoken to the directors. The storm days won't be held against the site in the client report; I've written them up as weather days, which is what they were. The client hasn't asked about the storm at all, which is very like them. Get some rest tonight while it's quiet. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: A forum post about an earlier job
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, it's come to my attention that a post on a local forum makes claims about a previous Grieve contract. I'd ask that you don't engage with it, and that the crew don't either, including by reading it out to each other. Previous jobs are a head office matter, and nothing about them has any bearing on the Holm. It's an ordinary clearance, just a big one. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Wages, again (sorry)
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, I'm sorry to raise wages a third day running. The balance has rolled into the new period and the directors have asked me about it by name, which they don't usually. I've told them the storm stopped everything, which is true. But it would help me a great deal if the next statement showed it moving. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Rota after the storm
units.author: ruth_imber
units.text: Hi, a short practical one. With the crew a person short and the storm having cost us days, there'll be a temptation to make it up with longer evenings once the wind drops. Please don't. Daylight hours only, everyone in at dusk, same as always. I'd rather explain a lower number to head office than a tired crew in the dark. Thanks, Ruth

units.title: Ammet District Council: your week (storm edition)
units.author: council_news
units.text: Storm clear-up: council crews are working through a list of more than sixty fallen trees on public land. The lower Tollinby road at Mill Bridge, the Brackwater ridge road and the Carrow Point road remain closed. Please report fallen trees on public land through the website, and don't attempt to move large branches from the road yourself.

units.author: council_news
units.text: Bins: general waste collections suspended during the storm will be caught up from tomorrow. Please leave your bin out on your usual day. Recycling: the Port Ammet blue-bin round is expected back on the road shortly now that the repaired vehicle has been returned. We apologise to residents of Rope Walk and Market Row for the delay, and thank them for their patience, and their letters.

units.author: council_news
units.text: Thank you: to the volunteers at Brackwater village hall and Tollinby community hall, who kept the rest centres running for two days with tea, blankets and phone chargers, and to everyone who checked on a neighbour. Planning: no applications were determined this week, as the planning team spent most of it clearing the car park.

units.author: council_news
units.text: Photo competition: our autumn theme, 'The Sound at Work', is still open until the end of the month. We've already had several entries of linesmen up poles in the rain, which the judges admire, though we'd remind everyone that the best photograph is one taken from a safe distance. Consultation: the harbour parking review closes in two weeks.

units.title: Correction to this week's newsletter
units.author: council_news
units.text: Correction: this morning's newsletter said general waste catch-up collections would begin tomorrow. Because some roads remain closed, catch-up collections in Brackwater and on the Tollinby ridge will begin the day after tomorrow. Port Ammet, Gilliver and Lisle collections will run tomorrow as stated. We apologise for any confusion.

units.title: Why did the pine tree get in trouble?
units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Chief. It was being knotty. Bird table survived the gale, I'll have you know, though it's now facing the other way and the boy says the birds 'prefer it'. Road job restarts tomorrow if the culvert's still there. Hope your camp's still pointing the right way round. Hal

units.author: hal_brannock
units.text: Also, I've been meaning to say something to you since the paper, and I keep starting it and stopping. Not tonight. Tonight just get some sleep while the wind's down. I'll write properly in a day or two. Don't worry, nobody's dying, I'm just bad at letters. Hal

units.title: it's gone quiet
units.author: sam
units.text: hi, it's gone so quiet here tonight it's almost worse than the wind. power came back at teatime, the fridge made its shuddering noise and Bea cheered like it had scored a goal. she's asleep in her costume, which is a tree made of green bin bags, because she says trees don't get changed. anyway. is it really fine out there? you'd tell me. love, S x

units.title: it's gone quiet
units.author: sam
units.text: hi, the wind's dropped and the whole street came outside at once to look at the damage, like a party nobody planned. Mr Abbot's fence is in our garden and our bin lid is in his. Bea helped him carry the panels back and now thinks she's a builder. anyway. is it really fine out there? you'd tell me if it wasn't. love, S x

units.title: Pilot report
units.author: sam
units.text: Pilot report, as requested by nobody: the tea towel has, as the vet promised, passed. I won't go into it. He's eaten nothing he shouldn't today, which is a record, mostly because he's spent the storm under the kitchen table with his back to the wall like a cowboy in a saloon. He sleeps on your jumper every night. I've stopped trying to wash it. S x

units.author: sam
units.text: one more and then bed. the Courier says your lot sat out the storm in your camp and the company says work was 'paused for safety'. I read it out to Mum and she said 'good, that's sensible', and then she was quiet for a bit, and then she asked if you'd got a proper coat. have you got a proper coat? S x

units.title: After the storm
units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Hello, sorry, it's me again. Our lift is back and the balcony door held, as I said. The quayside flooded this morning, two streets down from the dental practice, so we've closed for a day and I've been helping the lady from the noodle bar move sandbags. I'm fine. Please tell Tomas, if he asks. Is he sleeping, now that it's quiet? Ana

units.author: ana_reyner
units.text: Sorry, I meant to say thank you. I don't know if you pass on my messages, and I know you can't write back. But it helps me to send them to someone who can see him, even if it's only across a camp. I hope that isn't strange. Ana

units.title: Amber warning: final hours
units.author: met
units.text: Marrow Sound, 06:00 ST. The amber wind warning remains in force until 12:00 today. Westerly gale 8 to severe gale 9, gusting 50 knots on coasts, with squally showers. Overnight, a peak gust of 59 knots was recorded at the headland station and pressure fell to 971 hPa around 02:00. Take care with storm debris and damaged trees.

units.author: met
units.text: Warning update, 13:00 ST. The amber warning has been replaced by a yellow wind warning, valid until 12:00 tomorrow. Winds will ease this evening, giving a lull of several hours, before a trailing trough brings strong westerlies and squally showers from about 03:00, gusting 50 to 55 knots on exposed coasts. Do not mistake the lull for the end of the storm.

units.title: Tides
units.author: met
units.text: Tides, Port Ammet. High water 06:58 (4.7 m) and 19:21 (4.9 m). The surge is now decreasing, but tonight's high water remains the highest of the month. Minor overtopping is possible at the Gilliver harbour front and on the Port Ammet promenade, where shingle is still on the path. Gilliver and Lisle times about twelve minutes later.

units.title: Evening forecast
units.author: met
units.text: Evening forecast, 18:00 ST. Winds falling light this evening, variable at times, with clear spells. From about 03:00, westerly winds increase again to gale 8 on coasts with heavy, squally showers, easing through tomorrow afternoon. Minimum 5 C. Tomorrow: blustery at first, becoming calm and clear by evening, with frost possible inland.

units.title: Service update: limited sailings
units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 06:00. There will be no morning sailings today. We will run a single midday sailing from Port Ammet to Lisle and Gilliver, subject to an inspection of the Lisle slip at 09:00. A further update will be posted at 10:00. Please do not travel to the terminal until the sailing is confirmed.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 12:15. The midday sailing has departed Port Ammet. The 15:30 and 17:45 sailings will operate subject to conditions. The 20:15 will operate. Tonight's 23:40 and 00:55 night crossings are cancelled. Passengers with vehicles booked on cancelled sailings will be contacted directly.

units.author: ferry
units.text: Sound Lines, 20:30. Tomorrow's 07:10 sailing will be decided at 06:00 following the overnight forecast. Daytime sailings are expected to run. An update on night crossings will follow tomorrow. We thank passengers for their patience over the last two days.

units.title: Restoration: progress
units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op, 08:00. Overnight, crews restored supply to the Station Road care home and around 500 properties in Tollinby and Brackwater. About 700 properties remain off, mainly on the Brackwater ridge, where two poles are down across the lane, and in east Tollinby. If your neighbours have power and you do not, please report it.

units.author: power
units.text: Sound Power Co-op, 17:00. Supply has been restored across Tollinby. Around 400 properties remain off on the Brackwater ridge and in the reservoir hamlet. New poles are being delivered and we expect to restore most of these customers tomorrow. Brackwater village hall stays open until 22:00 with a generator and hot drinks.

units.title: Storm clean-up and collections
units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. Crews are clearing fallen trees across the district, starting with bus routes and school roads. Closed: lower Tollinby road at Mill Bridge (verge slip), the Brackwater ridge road near Holly Lane, and the Carrow Point road. The Tollinby road at the garden centre dip has reopened. Bin catch-up details are in this week's newsletter.

units.author: council
units.text: Ammet District Council. The Port Ammet promenade remains closed while shingle is cleared. Residents of the Gilliver harbour front may leave storm-damaged items for collection beside their bins tomorrow. Please keep sandbags in place until the yellow warning ends; they can be returned to Rope Walk Yard next week.

units.title: Storm debris and harbour status
units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. The storm warning has been lifted; a gale warning remains in force. Gilliver and Lisle harbours reopen to essential movements from 10:00. Mariners should expect floating debris, including fish boxes, timber, fenders and a partly submerged rowing boat reported south of Gilliver. Keep a good lookout and reduce speed in poor visibility.

units.author: coast
units.text: Coastguard, Marrow Sound. Navigational warning 15/1. The Lisle Spit east cardinal buoy, previously reported unlit, is now reported to have shifted during the storm. Its position is being checked. Vessels should give the spit a wide berth until further notice.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Dec. 11th. Frost. Felled 29. Rowe & Pascoe gone by the boat without their wages, Mr Trevail saying he will send them on. They took Hocking's chest which he left. Roster 15. Mr Trevail says the far line is to be left for the spring. The lamps kept in all night as ruled. The cook complains of the oil smell in the bread.

units.author: camp_clerk_1894
units.text: Dec. 13th. Snow showers. Felled 31. Lamp oil one gallon. The boat did not come, the wind against it. Oil rationed to the bunk-house lamp only, & the men sat up with it in turns. No man went out after dark nor was asked to. Tally for the fortnight 340. Roster 15.

units.author: naturalist_1923
units.text: Sixth day. Rain all day. Skins and notes in the curing-station cottage, which is dry but smells of brine. Hooded crows in pairs on every headland, the only common bird here that is not shy. As to the deer: I have now found a cast antler at the ridge spring, very old, green with moss [sketch: antler, five tines]. So deer were here once. It is the absence of the living ones that is odd.

units.title: Gilliver window lamp (wiki)
units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: The Gilliver window lamp is the custom of keeping a lamp lit in a front window from dusk until dawn. It is recorded since at least the 1880s.[1] Informants give varying reasons: a light for returning boats; 'so they know the house is awake'; a light for the dead; or simply good manners.[2][3] The custom declined after mains electricity reached the village in 1949 but never died out. It is a courtesy rather than a superstition, though informants disagree about to whom the courtesy is owed.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Talk. An editor has added 'the lamp was believed to ward off spirits', citing a 1972 holiday leaflet. Removed. None of the 1976 informants says 'ward off'. The nearest is tape 7: 'so they'd know the house was awake'. That is not warding. It is closer to manners. Please cite the oral history or the Rendle diary, which the Society holds, rather than leaflets.

units.author: hist_wiki_pell
units.text: Talk (continued). Marsh's 'during' is acceptable. I would add that the lamp rule may as easily have been a rule against drunken men wandering into a felling line after dark; camps of the period lost men that way every winter. Not every rule written down by lamplight is a ghost story. The diary's entry of 11 Dec., men leaving without their wages, rather supports my reading.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Agreed that it could be. The clerk's own phrase is 'beyond the lamps', not 'near the felling', and the men sat up with the lamp on 13 Dec. rather than going to bed early, which is odd for a rule about drink. I'll put both readings in a footnote and stop there, before we wear a hole in the talk page.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Feb. 2. Middle watch. Wind N.W. 4. Vis. good, moon. Lamp correct. Remarks: walkers again on the shore road, three this time, 03:20, standing below the wall and not walking. No lantern. Hailed. Did not answer. Assistant wished to go down. I said no. They were gone at 03:40.

units.author: carrow_keeper
units.text: Feb. 3. Middle watch. Calm. Visibility fell to 200 yards with fog from 02:00; fog signal sounded 02:05 until relieved at 04:00. Lamp trimmed twice. Remarks: none.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Tape 9, Mrs A. Dray. Q: You worked at the curing station? A: Gutting, from fourteen. Q: Did the women ever stay overnight on the Holm? A: Never. Season or no season. The boat took us off at five and brought us back at six. Q: Why? A: The cottage was for the foreman. Q: And did he stay? A: Some did. [laughs] Not for long. They'd come over to the Gilliver Arms of an evening and say it was the company they missed.

units.author: oral_history_1970s
units.text: Tape 10, Mr W. Hocking. Q: Your grandfather was at the timber camp? A: He was. Came home before Christmas and wouldn't go back for any money. Q: Did he say why? A: Wages. Said they weren't paid. [pause] Mind, he said that about every job he ever had. Q: Anything else? A: He kept a lamp in the back window as well as the front. Mother thought it a waste of oil.

units.title: Catalogue LBA-0221 (Brackwater, 2009)
units.author: lowband_archivist
units.text: LBA-0221. Date: spring 2009. Location: Brackwater Woods, the oak stand above the reservoir path. Kit: two omnidirectional microphones, solid-state recorder. Duration: 3 h 12 min. Content: dawn chorus from 05:50, tawny owls, rain on new leaves. Recordist: dunlin_rec, an early file from before his current series. No percussive events. Curator's note: the oak in this recording is still standing, and was checked after the storm.

units.author: courier_archivist
units.text: From the issue of 9 February 1953, page 3, a letter: 'Sir, after the gale I walked the Gilliver shore and counted eleven boats damaged and not one lamp out in the village, although the electric was off for three nights. Make of Gilliver what you will. A Visitor.' Editor's note: 'make of it what you will' turns up in these pages more often than you would expect.

units.author: hist_wiki_marsh
units.text: Talk. Pell's proposed wording is fair and I've adopted it. I'd add, from her own notebook, the cast antler at the ridge spring on her sixth day, which she records as 'very old'. That supports Pell's general point that deer could reach the Holm. It does not explain why, in good browse, she found no living sign of them. Both now in the article.

units.author: retired_teacher
units.text: I am delighted the herring prices have found a home, though less delighted to learn that 'hering' survived thirty-three years of my red pen. I shall take the folder to the Society myself once the ferry is reliable again, and I shall bring Ewan, who owes the archive a proper spelling of his grandfather's boat.

units.author: sb_commuter_lisle
units.text: The boat was the 'Margaret Ann', Mrs Hale, two words and an e on the end. I've known that since I was nine and I'll defend it at the Society if necessary. I'll carry the folder, if the midday ferry's still running by then. It was forty minutes late today and the saloon smelled of wet dog.

units.author: fisher_bram
units.text: Swept the harbour road with the lifeboat lads this afternoon, three barrow loads of weed and stones. Wind's dropped right off now, flat calm by eight. Lamp's lit at my aunt's and at mine. Creels go back out on the Holm side the day after tomorrow, if the trough doesn't make liars of the Met.
